The 1-year history of incontinence preceding gait decline aligns with MSA’s typical evolution—autonomic failure often precedes or coincides with motor signs. The MRI shows atrophy and signal abnormalities in the brainstem, cerebellum, and basal ganglia—classic for MSA (e.g., “hot cross bun” sign in pons, putaminal rim hypointensity, cerebellar atrophy). Critically, red flags for mimics are absent: no sensory symptoms (argues against spinocerebellar degenerations with dorsal column involvement or vitamin E/B12 deficiency), no visual changes (against SCA7, mitochondrial disorders), no bowel dysfunction (though urinary incontinence alone suffices for probable MSA), no spinal pathology (rules out structural myelopathy), and no evidence of inflammation/demyelination on MRI (argues against MS or ADEM). The absence of spasticity, fasciculations, or upper/lower motor neuron signs makes motor neuron disease unlikely. Progressive supranuclear palsy is less likely without vertical supranuclear gaze palsy, early falls, or axial rigidity—none reported. Prion disease is improbable without rapid progression (<2 years), cognitive decline, or 14-3-3 positivity (not yet tested, but clinical tempo—1 year to wheelchair—is subacute, not hyperacute). Hereditary ataxias remain possible but are *less likely* without family history or younger age onset (not specified, but 1-year insidious onset + 3-month acceleration is more typical of MSA than most SCAs, which usually evolve over years to decades). Thus, MSA—particularly the cerebellar subtype (MSA-C)—is the single most coherent, evidence-supported diagnosis.

[EVIDENCE]  
- Urinary incontinence began 1 year prior to presentation — early autonomic failure, a core feature of MSA.  
- Gait disturbance progressed to wheelchair dependence over 3 months — rapid cerebellar/brainstem motor decline, consistent with MSA.  
- Recent-onset dysarthria — reflects brainstem (pontine/cerebellar) involvement, typical in MSA-C.  
- MRI shows atrophy and signal abnormalities in brainstem, cerebellum, and basal ganglia — hallmark neuroimaging pattern of MSA.  
- No sensory symptoms — argues against many hereditary ataxias and metabolic causes (e.g., B12 deficiency).  
- No limb weakness, spasticity, or fasciculations — reduces likelihood of motor neuron disease, HSP, or inflammatory myelopathy.  
- No visual changes — makes SCA7 and mitochondrial disorders (e.g., MELAS, NARP) less likely.  
- No bowel dysfunction or orthostatic hypotension explicitly reported — but urinary incontinence alone meets probable MSA autonomic criterion (per Second Consensus Statement on MSA).  
- No spinal pathology — excludes compressive or structural etiologies.  
- No demyelination on MRI — argues against multiple sclerosis or other inflammatory CNS disorders.

[GAPS]  
- Absence of documented orthostatic hypotension (e.g., blood pressure measurements supine vs. standing) — critical supportive criterion for probable MSA.  
- No urodynamic study or formal autonomic testing (e.g., heart rate variability, Valsalva, tilt-table) — limits confirmation of autonomic failure beyond urinary incontinence.  
- Age of onset not specified — if <30 years, hereditary ataxia becomes significantly more likely; if >50, strengthens MSA.  
- Family history not addressed — essential to exclude autosomal dominant SCAs.  
- No assessment of parkinsonism (e.g., bradykinesia, rigidity, rest tremor) — though absent per summary, formal exam documentation would help distinguish MSA-P vs. MSA-C.  
- No DaTscan or cardiac MIBG imaging — could help differentiate MSA (preserved cardiac sympathetic innervation, abnormal DaTscan) from Parkinson’s or dementia with Lewy bodies.

[DIAGNOSIS]  
Multiple System Atrophy, cerebellar type (MSA-C)
